frames.source_quote: The cutter creates periodic oscillation bursts every 2.62 ms, and each burst rings at around 2-6 MHz with peak to peak amplitude of above 100V (limit of my scope). frames.main_point: Connecting cable shields to the building mains safety ground increased the EMI observed in this setup. Leaving the shield floating produced less interference than bonding it to mains earth.
frames.source_quote: I tried to connected the shields to my mains safety ground (yellow/green). I'm using stranded wires everywhere, but the mains ground is solid core, so I didn't expected great results, however, grounding this way actually made it even worse, I measured less interference when the probed cable's shield was left floating.

frames.thread_title: Shielding powerful HF EMI

frames.label: Bonding the shield to the plasma cutter's work clamp terminal didn't appear to help and might have made interference...

frames.subject: effect of bonding shields to plasma work clamp under HF EMI
frames.thread_title: Shielding powerful HF EMI

frames.label: Adding ferrite cores to all cables provided only modest EMI reduction against the HF-start interference
frames.main_point: Adding ferrite cores to all cables provided only modest EMI reduction against the HF-start interference. The improvement was insufficient to solve the problem on its own.
frames.source_quote: I also added ferrite cores on every cable, and it helps a little bit, but not nearly enough.
frames.subject: general efficacy of ferrite cores against strong HF EMI
frames.thread_title: Shielding powerful HF EMI

frames.label: A ferrite choke placed on the shield’s grounding lead can substantially reduce RF pickup, but only when its impedance...
frames.main_point: A ferrite choke placed on the shield’s grounding lead can substantially reduce RF pickup, but only when its impedance is tuned appropriately. Too few or too many turns/sleeves on the ferrite eliminates the benefit and the interference returns.
frames.source_quote: However, I noticed a significant change when I added a ferrite ring to the grounding wire where it connects to the shield. It made the LEDs dim almost completely, when connected to the mains ground (compared to when the shield was left floating), but only at a certain number of turns, but it would have no effect with more or less turns around the ferrite ring. I replicated the same results with a ferrite sleeve. One sleeve would dim the LEDs a lot, while adding more than one sleeve would negate the effect.
frames.subject: tuning ferrite impedance on shield ground lead for HF EMI suppression
frames.thread_title: Shielding powerful HF EMI

frames.label: Unbalanced loads on cabling can convert common‑mode interference picked up by the cables (acting as antennas) into di...
frames.main_point: Unbalanced loads on cabling can convert common‑mode interference picked up by the cables (acting as antennas) into differential noise on the signal lines. Treating cabling and loads with this in mind is key to mitigating EMI issues.
frames.source_quote: Consider all cables as antenna and loads as unbalanced (eg. LED) so common mode noise becomes differential.
frames.subject: common-mode to differential conversion in unbalanced loads
frames.thread_title: Shielding powerful HF EMI

frames.label: Use a common‑mode choke (balun) sized with sufficient inductance at the offending frequency to equalize the different...
frames.main_point: Use a common‑mode choke (balun) sized with sufficient inductance at the offending frequency to equalize the differential impedances, which reduces conversion of common‑mode noise into differential noise. Choose the inductance based on the EMI’s frequency content rather than a generic value.
frames.source_quote: The solution is to use a CM choke with high enough inductance to make each differential impedance more equal at 9MHz.
frames.subject: common-mode choke sizing to balance differential impedance (balun)
frames.thread_title: Shielding powerful HF EMI

frames.label: Shield capacitance can couple RF noise into signals; terminating the shield to a low‑impedance point at the end where...
frames.main_point: Shield capacitance can couple RF noise into signals; terminating the shield to a low‑impedance point at the end where interference is observed helps attenuate the coupled noise. Grounding/termination should be at the interference‑sensitive end for best effect.
frames.source_quote: Then the shield capacitance is coupling the antenna noise to the signals so it terminating to low impedance at the end where interference is detected should attenuate it.
frames.subject: shield termination strategy for HF EMI
frames.thread_title: Shielding powerful HF EMI

frames.label: At high frequencies, the parasitic inductance of ground conductors and the capacitance of cable shields can resonate,...
frames.main_point: At high frequencies, the parasitic inductance of ground conductors and the capacitance of cable shields can resonate, potentially worsening EMI instead of attenuating it. Expect this resonance based on typical per‑meter values for L and C in cabling and grounds.
frames.source_quote: But  at this frequency expect inductance (<1uH/m)of ground to resonate with shield capacitance (~<100pF/m) at some frequency.
frames.subject: resonance between ground inductance and shield capacitance

frames.label: If the line is just supplying DC to an LED, adding an RC snubber in shunt will provide additional attenuation

frames.subject: RC snubber to damp resonance/coupled noise on DC LED lines

frames.label: Use the cutter power unit’s main earth as the single reference point and return all connections to it via the lowest-...
frames.main_point: Use the cutter power unit’s main earth as the single reference point and return all connections to it via the lowest-impedance paths. This minimizes stray current loops and the resulting magnetic induction.
frames.source_quote: The key earthing point is the main earth point of the cutter supply power unit: everything needs to get back to that as directly and with as low an impedance as possible. This will minimise stray current loops and hence magnetic induction.
frames.subject: single-point earthing to minimize loop induction

frames.label: At around 380 kHz, either a star earth or a ground plane can be acceptable, but for interference in the 2–6 MHz range...
frames.main_point: At around 380 kHz, either a star earth or a ground plane can be acceptable, but for interference in the 2–6 MHz range (and higher from the plasma) a ground plane is essential. Frequency drives the choice between star and ground-plane earthing.
frames.source_quote: For the 380 kHz the earthing system is moot. A star earth might be OK, or a ground plane. But if the 2-6 MHz persists - and frequencies well above that will also be emitted by the plasma - then a ground plane approach is essential.

frames.label: When applying heavy shielding, accompany every signal line with its return line, and shield the pair with the shield...
frames.main_point: When applying heavy shielding, accompany every signal line with its return line, and shield the pair with the shield bonded (grounded) at both ends.
frames.source_quote: Basically, you go do indeed go mad with shielding, and every signal line must be accompanied by its return line, the pair shielded and grounded at both ends.

frames.label: Do not route any other lines through the loop formed by the HT supply, torch feed cable, torch, workpiece, and ground...
frames.main_point: Do not route any other lines through the loop formed by the HT supply, torch feed cable, torch, workpiece, and grounding cable.

frames.label: Poor joints or gaps in shielding add impedance in the return path, turning the less‑well‑grounded shield segment into...
frames.main_point: Poor joints or gaps in shielding add impedance in the return path, turning the less‑well‑grounded shield segment into an antenna. EMI is not simply leaking through openings; the discontinuity creates re‑radiation.
frames.source_quote: The enemy of shielding is poor joints. The EMI does not leak through the gaps, as commonly imagined, but the gaps create an impedance in the current path, turning the less-well-grounded piece of shielding into an antenna.
frames.subject: shielding gaps creating antenna effects
frames.thread_title: Shielding powerful HF EMI

frames.label: Blanket the setup with foil and ferrites until the interference ceases, then remove shielding items one by one to ide...
frames.main_point: Blanket the setup with foil and ferrites until the interference ceases, then remove shielding items one by one to identify which are necessary. If removing a piece brings the interference back, restore it and proceed to the next.
frames.source_quote: You can do a lot of shielding trials using cooking foil and sticky tape. The classic technique with shielding is to wrap everything in sight with silver foil and ferrite clamps, until the interference stops. Then remove each bit of the shielding in turn to establish which bits are actually needed. If a removal exposes interference, put it back and move on to the next bit.
frames.subject: iterative blanket-then-remove shielding test method
frames.thread_title: Shielding powerful HF EMI

frames.label: Use a short bipole probe or a small loop in place of the scope probe to scan for leakage sites; these highlight shiel...
frames.main_point: Use a short bipole probe or a small loop in place of the scope probe to scan for leakage sites; these highlight shielding gaps but not the true EMI source. This helps locate weak points in the shield enclosure.
frames.source_quote: Two useful probes for leakage sites, which can be fitted in place of the usual 'scope probe, are a short bipole (two stiff wires bent in opposite directions, one on the shield and the other on the signal line, or else a small loop connected across the two. These will highlight gaps in the shielding but not the "source" of the EMI as such.
frames.subject: using bipole or loop probes to find shielding leaks

frames.source_quote: If you think of it as a quarter-wave resonator, take the speed of signal propagation as 0.6 c (180 x 10^6 m/sec if I recall correctly, but do confirm that for yourself!), figure out the resonant frequency and look for that.

frames.label: In an NC configuration, a brief contact interruption is enough to trip a limit, while an NO configuration requires th...
